Seminar Title:

Effect of Different Peening Techniques on the Microstructural, Surface-Mechanical and Corrosion Behaviour of Electroplated Nickel Coating: A Hybrid Surface Engineering Approach

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Metallurgical and Materials Engineering

Speaker Name:

Sivasubramanian J ( Rollno : 521mm1003)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

MM202, Metallurgical and Materials Engineering Annex Building 1st floor.

Date and Time:

28 Aug 2026 04:30 PM

Contact:

Anindya Basu

Abstract:

Nickel coatings are applied to copper substrates to enhance their surface strength and corrosion resistance, particularly in aggressive chloride-containing environments. The electrodeposited nickel coatings provide higher hardness, wear resistance and corrosion resistance, thereby improving the performance of the copper substrate. However, the electrodeposition process can result in surface defects, inadequate coating-substrate adhesion, and tensile residual stresses, which can adversely affect the long-term mechanical properties and corrosion performance of the coating. Peening processes have been widely employed to induce plastic deformation and beneficial compressive residual stresses (CRS) in the near-surface region, thereby improving strength and overall surface integrity. Accordingly, the present study investigated the effects of conventional shot peening (CSP), ultrasonic shot peening (USP) and laser shock peening (LSP) as post-deposition surface mechanical treatments on the adhesion, mechanical properties, and corrosion behaviour of electrodeposited nickel coatings to assess their potential for developing an effective hybrid surface engineering process. The unpeened and peened nickel-coated samples were systematically characterised to evaluate their surface characteristics, residual stress, mechanical properties and scratch adhesion behaviour, and corrosion behaviour in 3.5 wt. % NaCl solution. The results demonstrated that peening significantly modified the nickel coating through coating densification, grain refinement, reduction of surface defects, and the introduction of beneficial CRS, which collectively improved the overall surface integrity of the coatings. These modifications improved coating adhesion and surface hardness, thereby enhancing the scratch resistance of the coatings. The reduction of surface cracks and defects limited electrolyte penetration into the nickel coating, while the induced CRS contributed to improved coating integrity, resulting in lower corrosion current density, higher polarisation resistance and enhanced corrosion resistance. The corrosion rate was substantially reduced from 0.8692 to 0.00684 mpy following USP treatment, while LSP decreased the corrosion rate from 2.961 to 0.02 mpy under the optimum peening condition. Additionally, the peened nickel coatings exhibited passivation at a lower potential and facilitated the formation of a stable protective passive film, which further increased their electrochemical stability. Overall, the results demonstrated that the appropriate selection of the post-deposition peening technique and optimisation of its process parameters effectively improved the surface integrity, mechanical properties, and corrosion performance of the electrodeposited nickel coatings.
